issues.item: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old whose index trauma is witnessing domestic violence in childhood, this appraisal is hard to reconcile with the likely role in the trauma. A child witness may feel guilty, but 'I should have protected others' implies a level of responsibility and agency that is clinically implausible enough to question for this trauma context. The rest of the profile coheres around fear, helplessness, fragmented sensory memory, and hypervigilant threat monitoring; this single appraisal stands out as inconsistent with the demographics/trauma role.

vignette:
Jamal, an 18-year-old African American man, had only recently joined the police force, a lifelong aspiration to protect and serve. Yet, beneath his crisp uniform lay a profound internal struggle, rooted in a childhood memory that continued to dictate his present. He was only six when he witnessed a brutal domestic dispute unfold in his home. He remembers hiding, small and terrified, as shouts escalated to crashes, and the terrifying silence that would follow an outburst, making him feel something truly dangerous was about to happen. He vividly recalls the glint of a kitchen knife, a snapshot memory that now makes him notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, an ingrained vigilance. During the chaos, he felt his small body tense, rigid and frozen, a bodily reenactment that still occurs when certain memories come to mind. He was utterly helpless, unable to intervene, a feeling that laid the foundation for his enduring belief that he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him.

The traumatic event left Jamal with a series of fragmented pictures in his mind, each a still moment of terror. When these painful images surfaced, an overwhelming grief would wash over him, a profound sadness for the innocence lost and the terror endured. This grief, coupled with the vividness of his memories, served only to deepen his conviction that he was helpless and couldn't rely on himself, reinforcing his negative appraisals of himself and the world. These persistent memories also made him feel as though the threat was still present, keeping him in a constant state of alert.

He had grown up with a deep-seated belief that he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him, a constant sense of helplessness that now, as an adult, translated into an amplified perception of threat. This conviction that he was fundamentally powerless to protect himself made the traumatic images of the knife and his frozen body replay in his mind, as if to constantly confirm his inability to act. This pervasive appraisal meant he was always on edge, feeling as if danger lurked just beneath the surface, feeding his hypervigilance. Moreover, his conviction that he couldn't protect himself made him exquisitely sensitive to any sign of discomfort or potential danger in his surroundings. This heightened vigilance meant he noticed potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, a habit that served him well as a police officer but felt like a curse otherwise.

Now, in his professional life, these old fears were magnified. A sudden, unexpected touch from a colleague in the precinct office would send a jolt through him, instantly bringing back the feeling of his body being frozen in that childhood moment of terror, as though his past self was re-emerging. Any situation where people acted suspiciously, even just a group loitering on a street corner, would trigger a wave of intense discomfort. This perceived threat would immediately pull him back to the fragmented pictures of his past, making him feel the danger was imminent and very real.

The intense physical and emotional reactions to these triggers, coupled with the persistent sense of threat, made Jamal increasingly worry that he was going crazy. This fear, a core negative appraisal, further intensified his perception of threat, making him even more vigilant. When he felt threatened, for instance, during a quiet patrol through an unfamiliar neighborhood, the unusual silence would make him feel something dangerous was about to happen, triggering vivid, bodily reenactments of the traumatic event. These distressing memories, in turn, reinforced his belief that he was helpless and couldn't rely on himself, deepening his negative appraisals. As a direct consequence of this heightened threat perception, he started avoiding going to unfamiliar places on his days off, feeling he couldn't properly assess the danger.

The belief that he couldn't rely on himself made him extremely sensitive to any perceived threat or discomfort, turning minor incidents into major internal alarms. This appraisal fueled his vigilance for suspicious behavior, making him see potential threats everywhere, even when none were present. Sometimes, even a fleeting memory of the event would make him overreact to a minor perceived threat, causing him to become excessively guarded during routine interactions, which impacted his ability to connect with the community he served. This memory-driven hypervigilance also made him more prone to misinterpreting neutral cues as triggers. Conversely, when he was in a state of heightened threat, his mind would involuntarily conjure up those vivid snapshot memories, making him feel as if the past was bleeding into the present. This feeling of current threat then made him even more attuned to potential triggers, creating a relentless and exhausting cycle.

The cumulative effect was profound. Jamal was constantly on edge, struggling to reconcile his desire to be a protective police officer with his internal sense of helplessness. His colleagues noticed his guardedness and his tendency to avoid social gatherings, especially in new venues. He felt isolated, trapped in a loop where every discomfort, every suspicious glance, every moment of silence threatened to pull him back into the past. It was this pervasive sense of being overwhelmed, and the creeping fear that his reactions meant he was truly "going crazy," that finally led him to seek help, hoping to find a way to break free from the past that still held him captive.

REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly convey how Jamal's negative appraisals directly influence or lead to his traumatic memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
